title: Kinetic Energy, Mass and Speed
keyIdea: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving. It increases in proportion to mass: twice the mass at the same speed means twice the kinetic energy. It increases with the square of speed: twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy, and three times the speed means nine times. So a graph of kinetic energy against speed curves upward, and small increases in speed cause much bigger increases in crash energy.

kid: Kinetic energy is the energy something has because it is moving. A still object has none. The faster it goes, or the heavier it is, the more it has. You can see this in a crash: more energy means a bigger dent.
Mass and energy go up in step. Put twice as much in a trolley, push it at the same speed, and it has twice the energy. Four times the mass gives four times the energy.

Speed counts more. Twice the speed gives four times the energy, because 2 × 2 = 4. Three times the speed gives nine times the energy. So on a graph of energy against speed, the line bends upward and gets steeper.
This is why speed limits matter. A car at 60 mph has four times the energy of the same car at 30 mph. In a crash, all that energy goes into bending metal and hurting people.
adult: This lesson meets NGSS MS-PS3-1: learners construct and interpret data to describe how kinetic energy depends on mass and on speed. The formula is kinetic energy = ½ × mass × speed², but at this stage the aim is the shape of the relationship (proportional to mass, proportional to speed squared), read from tables, graphs and a cart model rather than lengthy calculation.

The most common misconception is that doubling the speed doubles the energy. Learners treat speed like mass. Ask them to compare 1 m/s and 2 m/s for the same cart in the data, where the energy goes from 1 J to 4 J. A second slip is to think a heavy object always has more energy, even when it is moving slowly; the car against lorry and football against cricket ball comparisons show speed can win.

Be careful with graphs: some learners draw a straight line through the first two points and extrapolate. The table step asks them to predict 3 m/s and 4 m/s before the curve appears. Also make sure they know that a parked object has zero kinetic energy, however heavy it is, and that energy is measured in joules (J).

For road safety, connect the maths to real decisions: going from 20 to 30 mph raises crash energy about 2.25 times, which is why 20 mph zones near schools reduce serious injuries. Ask your learner to estimate how much more energy a car carries at 40 mph than at 20 mph.

familyTip: Roll a toy car down a ramp from low and then higher up, so it goes faster, into a pile of paper cups. Then tape a coin or two on top and roll it from the low spot again. Which made the bigger mess: more mass, or more speed?

visual.caption: What happens to the kinetic energy? Drag each change to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: load a cart with mass, change its speed, fill a data table, compare moving objects and crash-test a car.

practice.prompt: A shopping trolley moves at 1 m/s. You fill it so its mass doubles, and push it at the same speed. Its kinetic energy…
practice.hint: Mass and kinetic energy go up in step.
practice.explain: Twice the mass at the same speed gives twice the kinetic energy. Only speed is squared.

practice.prompt: A cyclist goes {k} times faster than before. Her mass stays the same. How many times bigger is her kinetic energy?
practice.hint: Speed is squared: multiply the change by itself.
practice.explain: {k} times the speed gives {k} × {k} = {=k*k} times the kinetic energy.

practice.prompt: A table shows a cart's kinetic energy at 1, 2 and 3 m/s: 1 J, 4 J and 9 J. What will the graph of energy against speed look like?
choices: A straight line through the points
A curve that gets steeper as speed goes up
practice.hint: Look at how much the energy goes up for each extra 1 m/s.
practice.explain: The jumps are 3 J, then 5 J. Each extra 1 m/s adds more energy than the last, so the curve gets steeper.

practice.prompt: A cart has {e} J of kinetic energy. You load it to {k} times its mass and keep the same speed. How many joules does it have now?
practice.explain: {k} times the mass gives {k} times the energy: {e} × {k} = {=e*k} J.

pool.prompt: Which has the most kinetic energy?
pool.hint: Mass counts once. Speed counts twice. Something still has none.
pool.explain: The 1 kg ball at 3 m/s has ½ × 1 × 9 = 4.5 J. The 4 kg ball at 1 m/s has 2 J, the 2 kg ball 1 J, and the still ball 0 J.

pool.prompt: A car speeds up from 30 mph to 60 mph. Compared with before, its kinetic energy is…
pool.explain: Twice the speed means 2 × 2 = 4 times the kinetic energy. That is why crashes at high speed do so much more damage.

pool.prompt: A parked lorry has a mass of 40 000 kg. What is its kinetic energy?
choices: Very large, because it is heavy
pool.hint: Kinetic energy is energy of movement.
pool.explain: It is not moving, so it has no kinetic energy, however heavy it is.

pool.prompt: Sam says, 'Doubling speed doubles kinetic energy, just like mass.' What is wrong?
choices: Speed is squared, so doubling speed gives four times the energy
Speed does not change kinetic energy
Doubling mass gives four times the energy
pool.hint: Look at 1 m/s and 2 m/s for the same cart: 1 J and 4 J.
pool.explain: Mass counts once, so it doubles the energy. Speed is squared, so doubling it gives four times the energy.

pool.prompt: A car going at 10 m/s and a lorry with 10 times its mass going at 3 m/s. Which has more kinetic energy?
choices: You cannot tell from mass and speed
pool.hint: Compare the multipliers: mass ×10 for the lorry, speed squared for the car.
pool.explain: Compare mass × speed². Car: 1 × 10 × 10 = 100. Lorry: 10 × 3 × 3 = 90. The car has slightly more, even though the lorry is 10 times heavier.

pool.prompt: Why are 20 mph zones used near schools instead of 30 mph?
choices: At 20 mph a car has under half the kinetic energy it has at 30 mph, so crashes do far less harm
Kinetic energy does not depend on speed
pool.explain: Energy goes with speed squared: 20² is 400 and 30² is 900, so 20 mph has less than half the crash energy.

pool.prompt: A ball has {e} J of kinetic energy. Its speed is doubled. How many joules does it have now?
pool.hint: Double the speed means four times the energy.

pool.prompt: A trolley's mass is multiplied by {k}. Its speed stays the same. How many times bigger is its kinetic energy?
pool.hint: Mass and kinetic energy go up in step.
pool.explain: Mass counts once, so {k} times the mass gives {k} times the energy.

pool.prompt: A runner's speed is multiplied by {k}. How many times bigger is her kinetic energy?
pool.hint: Multiply the speed change by itself.
pool.explain: {k} × {k} = {=k*k}, so her kinetic energy is {=k*k} times bigger.
